title: OneLake: The Unified Data Lake at the Heart of Microsoft Fabric
summary: OneLake is the single, tenant-wide logical data lake that underpins every Microsoft Fabric experience. This article explains the architecture, shortcut system, security model, and internal mechanics that make OneLake the common storage fabric for T-SQL, Spark, Power BI, and every other Fabric engine.
body_md:
## What Is OneLake and Why Does It Matter?

Every Microsoft Fabric tenant comes with exactly one OneLake, full stop — you cannot spin up a second one, and the one you have cannot be torn down [S2]. It functions as the organization's single logical data lake, sitting on top of Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, and every compute engine in Fabric is wired up to use it as its default store from day one [S1]. Microsoft's own comparison is to how Office apps quietly save into a user's OneDrive: the storage layer is simply present and unified, and nobody has to provision or babysit a separate resource for it [S1][S2].

For practitioners coming from a world of per-team or per-business-unit data lakes, this changes the starting point. Spinning up an independent storage account for every group used to be normal practice, but doing that now just reintroduces the duplication and operational overhead OneLake was built to remove — it has shifted from default approach to antipattern [S2].

Any data item in Fabric — a lakehouse, a warehouse, and others — writes its tabular data into OneLake as open Delta-Parquet files automatically, no matter which engine produced it [S2]. There's no manual "push to storage" step to remember. As soon as a lakehouse or warehouse exists, its data is already sitting in OneLake in an open, engine-neutral format.

![OneLake architecture, namespace, shortcuts, storage format, and security model](/diagrams/onelake-architecture.svg)

## Core Architecture: One Namespace, Every Engine

### A Single File-System Namespace

A Fabric tenant's OneLake is one continuous file-system namespace stretching across every user, region, and cloud the tenant touches [S1]. The tenant itself sits at the root of that namespace, workspaces hang off it the way folders would, and lakehouses and other items live inside those workspace folders [S1]. Under the hood, OneLake treats the whole tenant as though it were a single enormous ADLS storage account, with each workspace showing up as a container and each data item showing up as a folder inside its workspace's container [S2]. That makes every path in OneLake unique across the entire tenant — a Spark job and a T-SQL query that reference the same item are pointed at the exact same bytes, with nothing to reconcile.

Because OneLake speaks the standard ADLS Gen2 API and SDK surface, tools already built for ADLS — Azure Databricks, Azure Data Factory, custom code on top of the Azure Storage SDK — can read and write OneLake data with zero modification [S2]. This isn't a thin compatibility shim sitting in front of something else; it's the genuine wire protocol.

### One Copy, Multiple Engines

The real payoff of having one logical lake is that several Fabric engines can work off the same physical Delta-Parquet files without ever copying them: T-SQL, Apache Spark, and Analysis Services (which powers Power BI) all read identical data on disk, so nobody is stuck duplicating a dataset per engine or locked into whichever engine happened to load it first [S2]. That single architectural choice removes the recurring problem where a reporting copy drifts from the serving copy, which in turn drifts from the raw copy.

### Governance and Resilience

Governance in OneLake cascades down a hierarchy. Security, compliance, and data-management policy set at the tenant level apply automatically to anything stored in OneLake, and workspaces — each tied to a capacity in a given region and billed on its own — handle ownership and access decisions beneath that tenant-wide layer [S2]. On the resilience side, OneLake keeps data on zone-redundant storage wherever the region offers it, and capacities have the option to turn on business continuity and disaster recovery so data is also copied into a separate geography [S2]. Deletion isn't instant, either: files removed from OneLake sit in a seven-day soft-delete window, and Azure Storage Explorer or PowerShell can bring them back during that time [S2].

## Shortcuts: Connecting Data Without Moving It

### What a Shortcut Is

Think of a OneLake shortcut as a pointer: it lives at one path and resolves to data sitting at a different target path, possibly in an entirely different storage system [S4]. The symbolic-link analogy holds well — remove the shortcut and the target data is untouched, but rename, move, or delete the target itself and the shortcut breaks [S4]. The practical effect is that remote files and folders show up as though they were stored natively, which is what makes virtual data products possible without ever duplicating a byte [S2]. Any Fabric engine reading through the OneLake API treats a shortcut exactly like an ordinary folder — Spark, T-SQL, Real-Time Intelligence, Analysis Services, and even non-Fabric ADLS-compatible tools query through it with no special-case code at all [S4].

You can set up a shortcut from inside a lakehouse or a KQL database, doing it by hand in the Fabric portal or driving it programmatically against the OneLake shortcuts REST API [S4]. The target can be another spot inside OneLake itself — a different item, a different workspace, or even another tenant entirely through cross-tenant data sharing — or it can reach outside Fabric altogether to external stores. Verified targets include Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, Amazon S3, Dataverse, and Google Cloud Storage [S1][S2][S4][S6].

### Internal vs. External Shortcuts

An internal shortcut points at data living in another Fabric item — a lakehouse, warehouse, KQL database, SQL database, mirrored database, or semantic model — anywhere across the tenant's items and workspaces. The person reading through it is authorized using *their own* Entra identity, and that identity has to independently carry read permission on the target; there's no separate credential sitting in between [S4]. External shortcuts (pointing at ADLS Gen2 or S3, for example) work differently: authorization is handed off to a cloud connection that gets bound the moment the shortcut is created. Binding that connection is itself a privileged action, so someone without rights on the connection simply cannot stand up a new shortcut that depends on it [S4].

> [!WARNING]
> Reading a shortcut through a Power BI semantic model in DirectLake-over-SQL mode, or through T-SQL in delegated identity mode, doesn't carry the end user's identity through to the target — it uses the identity of whoever owns the calling item instead [S4]. Switch to DirectLake-over-OneLake, or to T-SQL's user-identity mode, and per-user passthrough comes back. It's an easy detail to overlook, and it changes who effectively gets access to the underlying data.

![OneLake shortcut identity passthrough decisions, delete-versus-write-through semantics, and the OneLake security role restriction matrix](/diagrams/onelake-shortcuts-security-internals.svg)

### Shortcut Caching and Performance

OneLake doesn't hit a cross-cloud source on every single read of an external shortcut — it keeps a cache scoped to each workspace specifically to hold down egress costs and latency. How long a cached file sticks around is tunable, somewhere between one and twenty-eight days, and that clock starts over every time the file is touched again. Any time the remote copy changes, the cache pulls a fresh version; once a file has gone untouched long enough to age out of the retention window, it's dropped; and anything over 1 GB never enters the cache to begin with. Coverage today extends to Google Cloud Storage, S3, S3-compatible stores, and on-premises data-gateway shortcuts [S4]. Writes skip the cache entirely and go straight to the source — it's strictly a read-side optimization.

### Documented Shortcut Limits

Fabric publishes hard ceilings here: a single item tops out at 100,000 shortcuts, no more than 10 shortcuts can sit on one OneLake path, and a chain of shortcuts pointing at shortcuts is cut off after 5 hops. The `%` and `+` characters, along with non-Latin characters, are also off-limits in shortcut names and paths [S4]. None of these are soft guidelines — plan data products to stay inside them instead of finding the wall in production.

## Security Model

### Two Planes: Control and Data

OneLake security splits into two distinct planes [S3]. The control plane decides what a user is allowed to *do* in Fabric — create an item, share a workspace, kick off a pipeline. The data plane is the OneLake security model proper, and it decides what data a user can actually *read*. The catch is that control-plane grants frequently hand out data access as a side effect [S3]: among the four workspace roles, Admin, Member, and Contributor can all read and write OneLake data without any extra setup, while Viewer is locked out of OneLake data entirely unless someone explicitly grants it through a OneLake security role.

Every identity check on the data plane runs through Microsoft Entra ID — that's true whether the caller is a person or a service principal — and Entra maps the authenticated identity onto whatever Fabric-defined permissions apply; turning on service principals at all requires a tenant admin to enable SPNs tenant-wide or scope them to particular security groups [S3].

### Hierarchical Permissions

OneLake permissions cascade down the same hierarchy as the storage itself: workspace, then item, then folder — including the `Tables/` and `Files/` folders inside a lakehouse — and anything lower in that chain inherits from its parent unless told otherwise [S3]. When data is shared at the item level, the scope of access depends entirely on which permission is granted: **Write** opens up both SQL and OneLake data access; **Read** hands out item metadata only and nothing more; **ReadData** unlocks the data itself, but only through SQL endpoints, including when those endpoints run in delegated mode; and **ReadAll** is the one that opens OneLake data directly, and only by way of the built-in DefaultReader security role [S3].

Every lakehouse comes pre-loaded with a DefaultReader OneLake security role, and anyone holding the ReadAll item permission automatically gets read access to the whole lakehouse through it; narrowing that down means going in and editing or removing the default role yourself [S3]. A OneLake security role itself has four moving parts — which data it covers (tables or folders), what permission it grants, which members it applies to, and any optional row- or column-level filters layered on top — and together those four pieces are what let you enforce table-, folder-, row-, and column-level security on lake data [S3].

### Encryption and Transport

By default, everything at rest in OneLake is encrypted with Microsoft-managed keys that rotate automatically and meet FIPS 140-2, and a workspace can opt to add customer-managed keys on top of that baseline if the organization needs to hold its own keys [S3]. Traffic coming into OneLake is required to use at least TLS 1.2, with TLS 1.3 negotiated automatically when the client supports it — but traffic going the other way, out from Fabric to infrastructure the customer owns, can quietly drop down to older protocols, even as far back as TLS 1.0, whenever the destination doesn't support anything newer [S3].

### Tenant-Level Controls and Auditing

There's a single tenant-admin switch that determines whether anything running *outside* Fabric — a homegrown client using the ADLS API, or the OneLake file explorer — is allowed to touch OneLake data at all. Flipping that switch off doesn't affect Fabric's own internal workloads, though; Spark and Data Warehouse keep working as normal [S3].

> [!NOTE]
> OneLake's audit log entries borrow ADLS-style operation names — `CreateFile`, `DeleteFile`, and the like — but the log has two blind spots: it never records read requests, and it never records anything routed through Fabric's own workloads [S3]. That's a meaningful hole to plan around in any compliance design that assumes a file system normally logs reads.

OneLake also lets third-party query engines plug into its security model directly — the "authorized engine" approach. An external engine registers with OneLake, pulls down the relevant security policy definitions and the access decisions OneLake has already worked out, and then enforces table-, row-, and column-level permissions itself, locally, at query time [S3]. That's the mechanism that lets Spark, T-SQL, and Analysis Services all honor OneLake security roles without phoning home to a central policy service on every single check, while still leaving OneLake as the one place policy is actually defined, for both Fabric-native and outside engines alike.

## Best Practices

**Let the single-copy model work for you.** The one-copy design is the core value proposition: load data once with Spark, query it with T-SQL, and serve it in Power BI Direct Lake, all from the same physical files [S2]. Resist staging intermediate copies of the same data across different items — that recreates the silo problem OneLake exists to eliminate.

**Use shortcuts to unify data without migration.** Rather than migrating everything into Fabric immediately, use shortcuts to bring existing ADLS Gen2, S3, Dataverse, or GCS storage into the namespace as live, read-only references, combinable with cross-tenant data sharing for governed external access [S1][S2][S5][S6]. Pipelines and notebooks operate on the shortcut path as if the data were native, while the source data stays exactly where it is.

**Scope security roles precisely, and know who they can't restrict.** The DefaultReader role is broad by design — appropriate for many scenarios, too broad for fine-grained control [S3]. Define custom OneLake security roles scoped to specific tables or folders wherever column-level or row-level restriction matters, but remember those roles only bind Viewers and ReadAll-share recipients, never the Admin/Member/Contributor workspace roles [S3].

**Use internal shortcuts for cross-team joins instead of copying tables.** Because internal shortcuts authorize against the calling user's own identity, a shared analytics lakehouse can shortcut into multiple team lakehouses and let OneLake enforce each user's existing permissions at the target, with no separate credential to manage [S4].

**Use the Windows file explorer for ad-hoc access.** For non-technical staff who just need to look at or grab a file, the OneLake file explorer for Windows surfaces every workspace and item the user can see and lets them upload, download, and edit straight from the desktop, no code required [S2].

## What Goes Wrong

**Siloed data lakes per business group.** Giving each team its own physical storage account, or carving OneLake workspaces into walled-off silos, is called out directly as an antipattern — it just rebuilds the duplication and the per-account upkeep that a shared tenant-wide OneLake with workspaces and shortcuts was meant to remove in the first place [S2]. If the goal is organizational separation, cross-workspace shortcuts achieve it without standing up another lake.

**Relying on OneLake security roles to restrict workspace roles.** The Admin, Member, and Contributor workspace roles sail right past OneLake security — full read and write on every item, no matter what a OneLake security role says on top of it [S3]. Fine-grained roles only ever apply to Viewers and to users who hold item-level Read. When particular people truly cannot see particular data, the answer is to put that data in its own item with its own sharing settings, not to layer a role inside a workspace those people already belong to.

**Spaces in shortcut table names.** Delta tables simply cannot have spaces in their names — so a shortcut created with one in its name will not register as a Delta table inside the lakehouse at all [S4]. It is an easy trap when shortcutting in tables from upstream systems that allow looser naming.

**Confusing shortcut deletion with delete-through.** Removing the shortcut itself only severs the link — the symbolic-link behavior holds, and the source data is left alone. Deleting a file or folder *through* the shortcut is a different operation entirely: if the caller has write permission at the destination, that delete propagates all the way to the source and the data is genuinely gone [S4]. Treat those as two different operations with opposite consequences, not interchangeable ways to clean up a shortcut.

**Assuming DirectLake-over-SQL passes the end user's identity through a shortcut.** Both DirectLake-over-SQL and T-SQL's delegated identity mode authorize shortcut reads as the item's owner, not as whoever is actually running the query [S4]. Any design that takes per-user passthrough for granted will quietly grant too much or too little access unless it's explicitly built on DirectLake-over-OneLake or T-SQL user-identity mode instead.

## Performance and Internals

*This section covers L4 depth — implementation-level mechanics relevant to optimizing high-volume or compliance-sensitive workloads.*

Underneath the portal, OneLake's addressing scheme maps each workspace onto its own ADLS container and each item onto a directory inside that container [S2]. A tool resolving raw ADLS paths against OneLake will run into this same predictable two-level hierarchy sitting under the tenant root — worth knowing if you're scripting against OneLake with the raw SDK rather than going through the Fabric UI.

For external shortcuts specifically, the per-workspace cache holds files for a tunable window of one to twenty-eight days, restarting that clock on each access; it evicts a file automatically once it ages past that window unused, refreshes automatically the moment the remote source changes, and refuses to cache anything bigger than 1 GB in the first place [S4]. Writes never touch the cache — they go straight to the target — because the cache exists purely to cut down on read-side egress and latency.

On the network side, inbound OneLake connections get TLS 1.3 whenever the client can negotiate it, but the outbound path — from Fabric compute back out to infrastructure the customer owns — can fall back to whatever the destination supports, including TLS 1.0 in the worst case [S3]. Anyone designing for strict transport requirements should check the actual Fabric compute surface in play rather than assuming TLS 1.3 holds tenant-wide.

Audit logging has a known gap to design around: OneLake records operations using familiar ADLS naming, but it simply doesn't log reads, and it doesn't log anything that came in through a Fabric workload [S3]. An audit program that needs read-level or workload-level attribution has to close that gap with a compensating control of its own — OneLake's native logging isn't enough by itself.

The authorized engine model is also what keeps fine-grained security fast at scale: query engines pull OneLake's security policy and pre-computed access decisions down locally and cache them, so row- and column-level enforcement happens inside the engine's own execution plan instead of as a remote lookup on every row [S3]. That's what stops latency from climbing as more engines start querying against the same OneLake security roles.

## Worked Example: Multi-Team Analytics Without Data Duplication

*Inference: the following scenario synthesizes multiple verified OneLake claims into one plausible end-to-end setup; the scenario framing itself is original, but every architectural step cites the claim it relies on.*

Consider a retailer with three teams — Supply Chain, Finance, and Marketing — each owning data in its own pre-Fabric ADLS Gen2 storage account, and a fourth, central Analytics team that needs to join across all three without copying anyone's data.

**Step 1 — Provision lakehouses.** Create a Fabric workspace per team; each workspace gets a lakehouse backed by OneLake automatically, with its tabular data persisted as Delta-Parquet regardless of which engine writes it [S2].

**Step 2 — Create external shortcuts to legacy storage.** In each team's lakehouse, create an ADLS Gen2 shortcut pointing at that team's existing storage container. The shortcuts surface as folders such as `Tables/supply_chain_inventory`, `Tables/finance_gl`, and `Tables/marketing_events` inside their respective lakehouses, with no data copied [S4]. Each shortcut's authorization is delegated to a cloud connection bound at creation time, so only users with permission on that connection can create or modify it [S4].

```text
lakehouse-supplychain/
  Tables/
    supply_chain_inventory/   <- ADLS Gen2 shortcut (external, cloud-connection auth)
lakehouse-finance/
  Tables/
    finance_gl/                <- ADLS Gen2 shortcut (external, cloud-connection auth)
```

**Step 3 — Build a cross-team view with internal shortcuts.** In a shared Analytics workspace, create a new lakehouse and add internal shortcuts pointing at the supply-chain and finance `Tables/` folders [S4]. A data engineer can now write a single Spark notebook or T-SQL query joining inventory against the general ledger, with OneLake transparently authorizing each internal shortcut read against the calling user's own identity rather than a shared credential [S4].

```text
lakehouse-analytics/
  Tables/
    inventory_shortcut/   <- internal shortcut -> lakehouse-supplychain (caller identity)
    gl_shortcut/           <- internal shortcut -> lakehouse-finance (caller identity)
```

**Step 4 — Secure the shared lakehouse.** Grant most analysts only **Read** access, which exposes item metadata alone and no actual data [S3]. For the handful of analysts who need to query the underlying tables through the SQL analytics endpoint without full file-level access, grant **ReadData** instead [S3]. For the two senior analysts who need direct file access, grant **ReadAll** and then narrow the default DefaultReader role with a custom OneLake security role scoped to the specific tables they need, rather than leaving the broad default in place [S3]. Do not rely on OneLake security roles to keep workspace Contributors out of anything — Contributor bypasses OneLake security entirely, so data that must stay restricted belongs in a separate item with its own sharing [S3].

**Step 5 — Confirm soft-delete coverage.** Before going to production, verify that an accidental deletion of a shortcut path is recoverable inside the seven-day soft-delete window using Azure Storage Explorer [S2], and confirm with the team which operation they actually intend — deleting the shortcut object itself (non-destructive to the source) versus deleting a file through it (write-through, and destructive at the source) [S4].
